synthesis.headline: Major Hurricane Trudy threatens southwest Mexico; eastern trough brings Northeast storms, wet snow, then frost
synthesis.narrative:
Hurricane Trudy is the main story. At 12Z it was a Category 3 with 120 mph winds and 956 mb pressure, about 240 miles southwest of Acapulco and moving northwest at 6 mph. NHC expects it to strengthen through Saturday and still be a major hurricane when it passes closest to the southwest Mexican coast Saturday night into Sunday. Most models keep the center offshore, but a small track shift would change the impacts a lot. A Hurricane Watch covers Punta San Telmo to Cabo Corrientes. Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco face 4-8 inches of rain, locally near 12, with life-threatening floods and mudslides plus surge and dangerous surf. Simon is down to 40 mph and fading west of Baja. In the US, an SPC Slight Risk covers the Mid-Atlantic into southern New England. A low-topped line forms around 17-21Z over eastern Pennsylvania and southern New York, bringing damaging gusts and a possible isolated tornado. Wet snow follows tonight over the lower Great Lakes and higher Northeast terrain.

Aloft, the pattern runs ridge-trough-ridge. A ridge over the interior West (up to about 592 dam) reaches into western Canada. Yesterday's open trough has deepened from the Upper Midwest to the western Gulf, with heights in the 540s-560s dam and 70+ kt jet streaks around it. Northwest flow between ridge and trough feeds an unusually strong 1043 mb high over the Rockies. It's in the 20s-30s behind the front, against 60s-70s in the Southeast, and a roughly 1000 mb Great Lakes low is deepening into southeastern Canada.

The trough moves into the Atlantic Saturday, with no severe threat anywhere. Frost and freeze concerns spread from the central US into the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast through Sunday. Next, a coastal low is expected to form off the Carolinas late this weekend, with likely high winds from North Carolina to Delaware; its strength is uncertain. Around Tuesday-Wednesday, a low should cut off over the West and pull in unusually deep moisture. That means heavy rain for the Four Corners and high-elevation Sierra snow. A central US ridge then brings warmth, with 80-90% odds of above normal near Wisconsin for Oct 21-25. CPC's charts say the eastern trough won't last. The 6-10 day chart has the western ridge retreating offshore over a -6 dam Southwest center, and the 8-14 day chart rebuilds +3 dam over western Canada and the East. With departures that small, the late-month regime is only loosely defined.
synthesis.climate_context: El Niño is now very strong. The JAS Oceanic Niño Index reached +2.16 C, up every season from -0.39 in DJF, though the warming has slowed lately (+1.39, +1.80, +2.16). The tropics fit that picture: the East Pacific is still active in mid-October with a major hurricane, a fading tropical storm and another likely system. Meanwhile NHC expects no Atlantic, Caribbean or Gulf formation for seven days. Over the continent, today's weather is a mid-latitude story: a typical mid-autumn amplified trough bringing early frost and first wet snow. El Niño's usual winter storm-track influence is not yet the driver.
synthesis.regional_notes: South Florida has WPC Marginal excessive-rainfall risks both days. Friday's covers the southern peninsula, and Saturday's narrows to the Palm Beach-Miami-Keys coast. No SPC mesoscale discussions are active. Simon brings 1-2 inches of rain to Baja California Sur through early Saturday. NHC gives a new low off southern Mexico a 60% chance of development next week. Satellite shows a compact high-PV dry tongue near Hudson Bay and Baffin Island along the polar jet.

sources.title: Surface Analysis
sources.summary:
This 1200Z analysis for Friday, October 16, 2026 is dominated by a strong continental high over the northern and central Rockies and High Plains. Three high centers are plotted, each near 1043 mb, one over Montana, one over Wyoming/western Nebraska, and one over Colorado and the central Rockies, with a further 1036 mb center over the Pacific Northwest and Idaho. The tightly packed isobars on the eastern flank of that ridge, running from the Dakotas through the central Plains and into the Texas Panhandle, mark the strongest pressure gradient on the map and imply a brisk northerly flow behind the cold front. Gradient is also visibly tight over the Pacific Northwest coast, where a deep system (labeled near 1013 mb at the edge of the chart) sits offshore with cold and occluded front symbols.

The main eastern feature is a low near 1000 mb over the eastern Great Lakes and Ontario, with a trailing cold front sweeping southwest through the Ohio Valley and Tennessee Valley, then along the Gulf Coast to southeast Texas. A warm front or frontal wave is plotted near the Mid-Atlantic coast, where several fronts converge close to Delmarva, and the plotted station reports suggest a compact area of active weather there. A cold front also trails offshore into the western Atlantic. The southern end of the Gulf Coast front is stationary or slow-moving as it approaches Texas, with a 1024 mb ridge axis along the western Gulf.

The temperature contrast across the main cold front is striking in the station plots: values in the 60s and 70s in the warm sector over the Southeast and Gulf Coast versus 20s and 30s over the northern Rockies and Plains. The pressure pattern is focusing lift along the cold front from the Great Lakes low down through the Tennessee Valley and Gulf Coast, with the most likely moisture convergence along the frontal zone in the Southeast and near the Mid-Atlantic coast. Behind the front, the strong dry high pressure suggests cold, dry, gusty conditions across the Plains.

The Four Corners and Southwest sit under slack gradient on the southern flank of the Rockies high, and the Florida peninsula also shows relatively weak gradients.

sources.title: Canadian Surface Analysis
sources.summary:
This CMC surface analysis for 00Z Thursday 15 October 2026 is a polar-projection chart, so the northern third of the frame is Arctic Ocean, the Canadian Archipelago and Greenland, and most of the deepest centers sit there rather than over the provinces. The strongest system I can read is the closed low near 944 mb in the upper right, which appears to lie over or just off the high Arctic and Greenland sector, with a second low of roughly 971 mb to its left and a 982-985 mb pair farther west near the central Arctic basin; because I cannot tie these to a specific coastline with confidence, I would call their positions Arctic rather than assign a territory. Over the Pacific Northwest and the Gulf of Alaska sector at left, a deep, tightly packed low near 969 mb shows strong gradient and an occluded front wrapping its south side, with a trailing cold front running southeast toward the northwest U.S. coast, and a separate low near 997 mb lies farther west at the chart edge.

For the cross-border pattern, a broad low near 98x mb sits over the western Canadian interior, with a well-defined cold front sweeping south and southwest along the Pacific coast toward the western U.S. and a warm front arcing east of it. Ahead of the system, highs of 1027-1030 mb over the Prairies and northern Plains look like a ridge axis in the continental interior, and the pressure gradient is tightest on the north and west flanks of the deep lows where isobars are crowded. Over southern Ontario and Quebec a front extends from a weak low near 1011 mb southwest toward the Great Lakes and into the Mississippi Valley, linking to a string of weak lows (1006-1017 mb) down the central U.S., which suggests a long cold front spanning the border region.

On the east side, a 1000 mb low near the Atlantic Canada coastline, with a cold front trailing southwest across the western Atlantic, marks the main focus for lift and moisture over the Maritimes and offshore waters, though I would treat the exact provincial placement of that low as approximate given the chart's small plotting scale. High pressure of about 1018-1026 mb behind it over the interior U.S. and eastern Canada indicates cooler, drier air building south of the border.

sources.title: 500 mb Analysis
sources.summary:
This 1200 UTC 16 October 2026 analysis shows a high-amplitude pattern: a ridge over the interior West and a deep trough over the central and eastern U.S. The ridge axis, marked by the H near the Idaho/Montana/Oregon area with contours near 580-592 dam, extends poleward into western Canada. The trough axis runs from the northern Plains/Upper Midwest southward toward the Mississippi Valley and western Gulf Coast region, with the chart's tightly packed height contours and shaded wind field implying a strong northwesterly-to-westerly jet on its western and southern flanks. Heights on the trough side fall into the 540s-560s dam, and a second subtropical ridge (the H at the right edge, over the western Atlantic) sits near 592 dam, so the pattern is a ridge-trough-ridge sequence across the domain.

The trough looks open rather than closed: contours wrap around it but I see no clearly closed low center within the domain, and the strongest height gradient lies on its back side, so it reads as a deep, amplified longwave trough still embedded in the westerlies rather than a self-retaining cutoff. Its orientation looks neutral to slightly positive, running roughly north-south to northeast-southwest from the Great Lakes toward the Gulf of Mexico, though the northern portion of the trough lies at the chart's upper edge and its geometry there is only partly visible.

Two wind maxima stand out in the shading. One is a jet core over southern Canada and the northern Plains (the dark red 70+ kt area at the top), and the other is a distinct streak over the Great Lakes/Ohio Valley region, both oriented roughly southwest-to-northeast. These suggest a strong cyclonically curved jet wrapping the base and eastern side of the trough, with a possible jet-streak coupling over the Midwest, though the chart alone does not show vertical motion.

The flow is not progressive in the classic zonal sense: the western ridge and eastern trough form a quasi-stationary, meridionally amplified couplet, with another ridge downstream near the Atlantic coast. This is not a Rex block, since there is no cutoff low beneath the western high. It is better described as an amplified ridge-trough couplet with moderately strong westerlies on its northern and western side, a configuration that tends to persist and sharpen temperature contrasts between a cold central and eastern U.S. and a mild West.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB (GOES-19)
sources.summary:
The dominant feature is a broad band of dry, red-orange upper-tropospheric air running from the northern Plains and Upper Midwest southwest-to-northeast across the Great Lakes toward southern Ontario and Quebec, with its sharpest saturation over Minnesota, Wisconsin and northern Michigan. A well-defined edge separates this dry air from the greener, moister air to the south, trending from the central Rockies and Four Corners region through Oklahoma and the Mid-Mississippi Valley to the Ohio Valley and central Appalachians. That sharp gradient marks the likely jet corridor, and the thin cloud streaks along it, notably over the southern Plains and Missouri, are consistent with the implied upper-level flow. The dry air looks broad rather than compact, so I would call it a dry upper-level airmass, not a stratospheric intrusion; a sharper dry feature may exist on the Pacific side, where deep red-orange fills the Southwest and northern Mexico.

Deep, cold-topped cloud shows a baroclinic leaf over Texas and the southern Plains, bright along the south side of the dry boundary. In the Northeast and Atlantic Canada, higher cloud lines the northern edge of the airmass boundary. The Southeast, mid-Atlantic and western Atlantic are dominated by green, moist tropical air with little organized convection.

The most vigorous deep convection sits in the tropics: a large, bright cloud mass over the northwest Caribbean off the Yucatan and Honduras, scattered cells over the southern Gulf of Mexico, and clusters near Hispaniola and off southwest Mexico in the Pacific. The Caribbean cloud mass looks the most organized, but this single image does not establish whether it has a closed circulation. At the far upper left, the purple and blue limb of the disk is a viewing-angle effect over the Pacific, and the white banding there appears to be cold high cloud.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB Full Disk (GOES-19)
sources.summary:
The most organized tropical feature is a compact cyclonic swirl with a small white convective core in the eastern Pacific, southwest of southern Mexico and roughly off the Guerrero to Oaxaca coast, with a curved cloud band wrapping toward the coast; its structure suggests a tropical storm or hurricane, though intensity cannot be read from this product. Elsewhere in the tropics, the main convective clusters sit over the western Caribbean and Central America, along the Colombian and Panamanian Pacific coasts, and over northwestern South America and western Amazonia. Cloud shields over Hispaniola and Cuba and scattered clusters in the tropical Atlantic appear less organized, with no other closed circulation evident.

At high latitudes the polar-jet signature is an arc of cold-dry blue and purple with a bright cloud band curving from northern Quebec and Labrador out over the North Atlantic, with an orange-red dry tongue just west of it near Hudson Bay and Baffin Island. That orange-red feature is compact and elongated on the cyclonic side of the flow, so it is consistent with a stratospheric-intrusion or high-PV signature along the trough, and the adjacent cloud band implies the jet and frontal corridor. Across the Canadian prairies and the Arctic coast the image shows mostly muted green and brown tones with scattered cloud, with no strong dry-intrusion signal evident near the limb.

The broad green moist tropical airmass fills most of the Atlantic and Pacific tropics, with a dark green moist tongue curving over the western Atlantic off the southeast US. Broad orange-brown areas over the subtropical Atlantic east of the Caribbean and the tropical eastern Pacific represent dry, likely subsident air under the subtropical ridges, rather than stratospheric intrusion. In the Southern Hemisphere, a large occluded cyclone spiral over the South Pacific near the bottom-left limb and a cloud mass off southern Brazil and Uruguay mark the mid-latitude frontal systems.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day Temperature Outlook
sources.summary:
This CPC outlook for October 21-25, 2026 shows the highest odds of above-normal temperatures centered on the Upper Mississippi Valley and western Great Lakes. A closed 80-90% contour sits over Wisconsin and adjacent parts of northern Illinois, eastern Minnesota and Iowa, with a broad 70-80% shield covering the Dakotas, Nebraska, Missouri, Illinois, Michigan and Indiana. Probabilities taper eastward and westward from there: 50-70% across Texas, the central and southern Plains and the Ohio and Tennessee Valleys, and 33-50% along the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic coasts, the Northeast, and the northern Rockies and High Plains. Maine and the interior of Alaska are shaded near normal.

The only below-normal signal is in the West, a 33-40% area covering most of California and Nevada, with a small 40-50% core over eastern California and western Nevada, bordered inland by a near-normal strip. Even the cool side is weak, so the chart favors warmth over most of the country without suggesting any strong cold anomaly.

This is a probability map, not a temperature or height map, so any upper-air reading is inference. The pattern is consistent with a western trough and a central-to-eastern ridge, with the warmest odds well downstream of the cool Western signal. The orientation of the probability bands, running roughly north-south through the Plains, points the same way. Because the cool signal is shallow and the near-normal buffer lies just to its east, any ridge-trough couplet implied here looks fairly progressive rather than locked in.

On persistence, the chart can only say that the odds for days 6-10 favor the existing warm-east, cool-west arrangement. It does not show whether the pattern holds beyond day 10. The eastward fade of warm probabilities toward the Atlantic coast and the modest cool signal in the West leave room for the trough to advance and erode the central warmth later, but that is speculation beyond what this single chart supports.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This is the CPC 6-10 day 500 mb height and anomaly prognostic, made 15 Oct 2026 and valid Oct 21-25. Heights are solid green contours labeled in meters (5100, 5160, 5400 through 5880, i.e. 510-588 dam), and anomalies are dashed at 60 m (6 dam) intervals, so the plotted -60 and 30 values are meters, equal to -6 and +3 dam. The chart's labels give no sign of 6-10 day forecast anomalies being larger than that.

The strongest negative centers are over the high Arctic near the pole (about -60 m, a closed 5100 m low) and east of Greenland (about -60 m). Positive anomalies are weak by comparison: closed red centers of roughly +30 m (+3 dam) sit over the northeast Pacific off the Canadian and Alaskan coast and in the Gulf of Alaska region, with a smaller positive area over the eastern Canadian Arctic and the Labrador/Quebec side. A separate negative center (blue, around -6 dam in the closed contour) lies over the Southwest and northwestern Mexico, with the zero line enclosing it over the Great Basin and southern Rockies.

The height field shows a broad ridge off the Pacific Northwest coast, with contours bowing north toward Alaska and the Yukon, then a trough axis dropping through the West and Southwest, consistent with that negative center. The zero-anomaly line runs along the Pacific Coast and reaches into the interior West, so positive anomalies are confined to the offshore Pacific and the far northwest, not over the western interior. That points to the western ridge retreating westward and northward compared with a continental-scale ridge.

East of the Rockies, the 5640-5700 m contours run roughly west to east across the northern tier and the southern 5820-5880 contours lie across the southern states, so the flow over the central and eastern US is fairly zonal, with only weak anomalies and a modest ridge over the Great Lakes and Northeast. The pattern leans toward a flattening of the flow across the lower 48, and I would not read a strongly amplified wave from this chart.

sources.title: CPC 8-14 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This is the CPC 8-14 day 500 mb height and anomaly outlook, made 15 Oct 2026 and valid Oct 23-29. Solid green contours are heights, labeled in meters (5160 to 5880 m, i.e. 516-588 dam), and dashed lines are anomalies at 60 m (6 dam) intervals. Red dashed lines are positive departures and purple and blue are negative.

A positive anomaly is clearly present over western Canada, spanning northwestern Canada and the Yukon, with the closed red contours labeled 30 m (3 dam) centered roughly over the British Columbia and Alberta interior and Pacific Northwest. A second, broader positive area covers the north-central and eastern United States and the Southeast, with a labeled 30 m contour east of the Mississippi. Positive departures therefore extend from western Canada across the northern Plains and Great Lakes, so the ridge is not retreated toward the Southwest: the contours curve northward through western Canada, and the heights near the Southwest and northern Mexico (south of 5820 m) look near zero or slightly negative.

The negative anomalies sit well to the east and west. A purple zero contour closes over the Gulf of Alaska and far northeast Pacific, while a negative center with a blue contour (below -60 m, i.e. about -6 dam) lies over Greenland and the Davis Strait region.

The flow is a strongly amplified western ridge with a downstream trough near Greenland. The implied northwesterly flow over central and eastern Canada is consistent with a sharp ridge-trough couplet, though there is no direct jet analysis here. Contours are tightly packed across the northern US and southern Canada, suggesting the strongest westerlies run along the Canadian border.

sources.title: Excessive Rainfall Outlook (Day 1)
sources.summary: This Day 1 Excessive Rainfall Outlook, valid 12Z Friday October 16 through 12Z Saturday October 17, 2026, shows a single risk area: a green Marginal zone (at least 5% chance of rainfall exceeding flash-flood guidance within 25 miles of a point). It covers the southern Florida peninsula, extending from roughly the Gulf coast near the Fort Myers area across to the Atlantic side around the Palm Beach and Miami corridor, with its northern edge somewhere around the middle of the peninsula. No Slight, Moderate or High risk areas are drawn anywhere, so Marginal is the highest category on the chart, and the rest of the contiguous US carries no excessive-rainfall risk. The chart does not show what is driving the risk, so I can't tie it to a tropical system, front or terrain from the image alone. The placement over low-lying peninsular Florida, with no terrain to speak of, is consistent with a moisture-rich, convectively active regime, but that is an inference rather than something plotted. Only the risk category is shown, not rainfall totals.

sources.title: Excessive Rainfall Outlook (Day 2)
sources.summary: This Day 2 outlook, valid 12Z Saturday Oct 17 through 12Z Sunday Oct 18 2026, shows a single risk area: a Marginal (at least 5%, green) zone. It is a narrow north-south strip along the southeast Florida coast, running roughly from the Palm Beach area southward past the Miami metro to the southern tip of the peninsula near the Keys, with the "MRGL" label sitting just off the coast over the Atlantic. No Slight, Moderate or High categories are drawn anywhere on the chart, and the rest of the contiguous United States is blank, meaning no excessive rainfall risk is outlined elsewhere. The thin, coast-hugging shape suggests the concern is tied to a low-level moisture or convergence axis near the Atlantic coastline rather than a broad system. A Day 1 comparison is not evident from this chart alone, so I can't say whether the risk has grown, shifted or relaxed.

sources.title: WPC Short Range Forecast Discussion
sources.summary:
As of 234 AM EDT Friday, October 16, 2026 (valid through 12Z Sunday, October 18), a deepening low tracks from the Great Lakes into southeastern Canada through Friday, driving a strong cold front across the eastern U.S. through Saturday. Gulf moisture ahead of the front fuels showers and storms from the Southern Plains to the Northeast.

Friday brings a severe thunderstorm risk across the Mid-Atlantic into Southern New England, with damaging wind gusts and a brief tornado possible. Wet snow develops over the lower Great Lakes and higher Northeast elevations late Friday into Saturday morning.

Flash flooding risk covers Florida Friday and Saturday due to repeated heavy rain, with storms also continuing over the Carolinas and Florida Saturday. Light showers reach the Pacific Northwest early Saturday.

Canadian high pressure builds southeast behind the front, bringing well below-seasonal temperatures to the central U.S., then spreading east. Overnight lows may approach freezing in the central U.S., with frost and freeze concerns expanding into the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast Saturday into Sunday.

sources.title: SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook
sources.summary:
SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook, issued 0742 AM CDT Friday, October 16, 2026, valid 1300Z October 16 to 1200Z October 17. A slight risk of severe thunderstorms covers parts of the Mid-Atlantic into southern New England, mainly this afternoon and early evening.

The main hazard is damaging wind gusts, with an isolated tornado possible. An upper trough amplifying over the eastern U.S. and a cold front sweeping east-southeast are the drivers. Isolated gusty convection may occur this morning along the front in western PA and NY. A low-topped line is expected to form by 17-21Z from central into eastern PA and southern NY, then spread quickly east. Damaging winds are most likely across eastern PA into NJ and southern NY, where instability is locally greater. MLCAPE is forecast at 500-1000 J/kg, but poor lapse rates limit updraft strength, and convection into southern New England may produce little lightning. Veering low-level flow may reduce effective SRH, so the tornado threat is limited. Convection should weaken by early evening as the marine layer and nocturnal cooling take hold. Severe probabilities were changed only slightly from the prior outlook.

sources.title: SPC Mesoscale Discussions
sources.summary: No SPC mesoscale discussions have been issued in the past six hours. No organized convective threat is currently being actively monitored by the Storm Prediction Center. No as-of time or staleness warning was included with this product.

sources.title: NHC Tropical Weather Outlooks
sources.summary:
Atlantic (as of 800 AM EDT Fri Oct 16, 2026): Tropical cyclone formation is not expected in the North Atlantic, Caribbean Sea, or Gulf of America during the next 7 days.

East Pacific (as of 500 AM PDT Fri Oct 16, 2026): Two active systems are being advised. Tropical Storm Simon is a few hundred miles south-southeast of the southern tip of Baja California. Hurricane Trudy is a few hundred miles southwest of Acapulco, Mexico.

A separate area of low pressure is expected to form offshore of southern Mexico in the early to middle part of next week. Conditions appear conducive for gradual development afterward, and a tropical depression could form in the latter half of next week while moving generally westward to west-northwestward across the eastern and central East Pacific. Formation chance is near 0 percent through 48 hours and 60 percent (medium) through 7 days.

sources.title: NHC Active Storm Advisories
sources.summary:
As of 12:00 UTC Oct 16, 2026, Hurricane Trudy is a major hurricane (Category 3) about 240 miles southwest of Acapulco, Mexico. Its center is near 14.5N 102.5W, moving northwest (325 degrees) at 6 mph, with maximum sustained winds of 120 mph (105 kt) and a central pressure of 956 mb. Hurricane-force winds extend 30 miles from the center and tropical-storm-force winds 140 miles. The track brings the center near the southwest and west-central Mexican coast Saturday, passing near the coast Saturday night into Sunday. Forecasters expect Trudy to strengthen through Saturday and remain a major hurricane at closest approach, then weaken later in the weekend as shear increases. The discussion (as of 09:00 UTC) says most models keep the center offshore, but small track changes could greatly alter impacts. A Hurricane Watch is in effect from Punta San Telmo to Cabo Corrientes, and a Tropical Storm Warning from Manzanillo to Zihuatanejo. More watches and warnings are likely. Forecast rainfall is 4 to 8 inches, with isolated totals near 12 inches, in Michoacan, Colima, and Jalisco, posing life-threatening flooding and mudslides. Guerrero may see 2 to 4 inches, isolated 6 inches. Storm surge, destructive waves, and life-threatening surf and rip currents are expected along the coast.

As of 09:00 UTC Oct 16, 2026, Tropical Storm Simon is weakening, centered near 20.0N 108.8W, about 210 miles south-southeast of Cabo San Lucas, moving northwest (310 degrees) at 9 mph. Maximum sustained winds are 40 mph (35 kt), with a central pressure of 1002 mb. Tropical-storm-force winds extend 25 miles. Simon is expected to become a post-tropical remnant low within about 24 hours and dissipate within about 48 hours, passing just west of the Baja California Peninsula. No coastal watches or warnings are in effect. Rainfall of 1 to 2 inches, with isolated maxima near 3 inches, is expected through early Saturday over Baja California Sur. Swells may affect west-central Mexico and Baja California Sur, bringing life-threatening surf and rip currents.

sources.title: ENSO State (Oceanic Niño Index)
sources.summary: The Oceanic Niño Index shows El Niño conditions in place and strengthening. The most recent season, JAS 2026, is at +2.16 degrees C, which is above the +2.0 threshold CPC uses for very strong events. Anomalies have risen every season since DJF 2026, when the index was -0.39, a La Niña-leaning value. The sequence runs -0.21 (JFM), +0.11 (FMA), +0.46 (MAM), +0.95 (AMJ), +1.39 (MJJ), and +1.80 (JJA) before reaching +2.16. The warming is steady, with the rate of increase slowing somewhat in the most recent seasons (from +1.39 to +1.80 to +2.16). The table gives no as-of date and no staleness flag, so the currency of these values can't be confirmed from the product alone.

sources.title: Teleconnection Indices (PNA, AO, NAO)
sources.summary:
As of 2026-09-30, the most recent teleconnection values are stale: CPC has not updated the table, and the newest reading is 16 days old, so these should not be treated as current.

PNA was +0.12, with the 7-day mean at -0.41, up from -1.51 the prior week. That is a rise from a negative phase toward neutral, which would weakly favor western North American ridging if it persisted.

AO was -0.26, with the 7-day mean at +0.04, down from +1.73. The index fell from strongly positive toward neutral and slightly negative, which would weakly favor high-latitude blocking if it continued.

NAO was -0.78, with the 7-day mean at -0.15, down from +0.28. The index has been falling and turned negative, which would weakly favor blocking that could help an eastern cutoff escape.

These are observed summer values, and extratropical teleconnections are weaker in summer, so treat them as directional support only.
